Male bladders have a capacity up to 400-600mL.
Female bladders have a capacity up to 300-500mL.
The detrusor muscle is the smooth muscle in the bladder wall that contracts during urination.
The internal urethral sphincter (involuntary) and the external urethral sphincter (voluntary) help control the release of urine.
As the volume in the bladder fill up to about 100-150mL, stretch receptors activate low-level signals, one typically becomes consciously aware around 300-400mL. As the volume in the bladder reaches 400-600mL, signals to the pontine micturition centre intensify, the urge to pee becomes stronger, and voluntary control becomes harder.

This switch from tension to relaxation is physiologically soothing, and can feel similar to emotional catharsis. The pudendal and pelvic nerves, involved in both urination and sexual arousal, are highly sensitive. Some of the same neural pathways used for sexual pleasure are involved in the sensation of releasing a full bladder. That’s why a really good pee can trigger a faint tingle, shiver, or goosebumps — sometimes called a “pee shiver” (technically post-micturition convulsion syndrome, a real but poorly understood phenomenon).

You've been neglecting your hydration. Momo stares at you with a fiery look in her eyes and her hands on her hips.

"Master, you always forget to drink water when you're busy. Here! Take a break and drink some of this." She nags at you even from within the comfort of your own home, handing you a glass of water.
